blocks.html: Strengths to Overcome: 3 of 4 competitors are now owned by major beverage capital (Diageo owns 2 of these companies), we cannot compete with global distribution and budgets right now.
Weakness to Exploit: Not many companies own true alcohol free drinks or authentic global drinks. Lyre's is 0.5% ABV, not alcohol free, Ritual is American classics only.
Opportunity to Pursue: All four analyses found the same demand shift, people are moderating, not quitting. That is something we can persue.
Threat to Prepare for: The TTB's 0.5% labeling line plus a 50% aluminum tariff (starting in June 2025) and a separate import tariff raise real cost and compliance pressure.

blocks.html: We understand there may be some ethical questions about Ar0und using recipies from around the world. We aim not to steal these recipies by any means but to simply make them accesable for all, regardless of whether or not they consume alcohol. Our team works one on one with bartenders from each drink's country of origin to create a completely authentic recipie. These partners are longterm relationships that we build and maintain throught the entire process and after. Partners recieve a percentage of profits on top of compenstation for the recipies and credit on the package. As for the cans themselves, we always, make sure the country of origin is on the cover in bold, to give credit where its due.

As Ar0und does create authentic cultural drinks, sometimes the ingredients required to maintain that quality require outsourcing. This importation has an environmental impact that we believe is important to acknowledge. We are very commited to reducing our emmisions from shipping and manufacturing through instead building more sustainable direct trade relationships. Partners will be clearly posted on our site for complete transparancey. We work with distributors to choose the least impactful method of shipping and choose to use only recycled materials for our cans and boxes. While this does contribute to a higher price, we prioritize paying our partners fairly. Typically growers and distributors can see small percentages of the final profit, but we are comitted to changing that norm by prioritizing their cut first and foremost. While this is something we are proud of, we would also like to acknowledge that this effects the price that customers pay. The price reflects our decision to never cut corners or unfairly pay our partners and we hope that those goals are also important to our customers.
Ar0und is built on the love our team has for culture and food. We believe that culture should be shared and we hope to encourage people to learn and seek out more culture from the world.

sections.html: Our responsibility doesnt end at the drinks, it extends to all the people whose recipies and Ingredients helped make Ar0und possible. Our responsibility is also always to our customers to be transparent and ethical.

sections.alt: Customer persona card. Meet Carlos, the travel-minded, alcohol-free explorer. Cut back on drinking to feel better and stay fit, but still loves going out. He wants drinks that taste like the real thing and flavors that remind him of his trips. Age: 25 to 34. Education: Bachelor's. Work: Freelancer. Travel: a few trips a year.

blocks.html: He doesn't want a mocktail. He wants an exciting drink that happens to be alcohol-free.
Carlos has expendable income and travels a few times a year, usually to cities where he can try street food and local drinks. He loves learning about new cultures and connecting on social media.
He cut back on alcohol to feel better in the mornings and stay on top of his health. He still loves going out with friends though and does not want to give up ordering something good while out.

items: Well crafted, fully alcohol free mocktails that are not just juice.

sections.text: What hinders that in the current market:

sections.html: The current availble NA drink options are often too sweet or too bland and many actually do conatin alcohol. Bars treat NA drinks as an afterthought causing carlos to feel left out and frustrated at the limited decisions.

Carlos scrolls Instagram and TikTok daily and saves recipe and drink videos to try later. He goes out with friends regularly and makes drinks at home on weekends. He shops online, reads reviews on Google and TikTok before trying new products, and shares things he likes on his own accounts.

blocks.html: Taste comes first, especially drinks that aren’t overly sweet. After that he looks at ingredient quality, price compared to a regular cocktail, how easy it is to buy, and whether it looks good enough to post.

He’s been let down by bland alcohol-free drinks before, so he’s skeptical of new ones. He also thinks many are overpriced for what they are and sometimes wonders why he shouldn’t just order a soda. If a product isn’t easy to find online or in stores near him, he’s unlikely to go looking for it.
Instagram and TikTok creators, online reviews, and recommendations from friends he travels with. A recommendation from someone he trusts carries the most weight.

sections.html: Carlos doesn’t know Ar0und yet, but he’ll most likely discover it through a creator video or a friend’s post. He’ll choose it over other options if the taste lives up to what’s promised and the brand gives him recipes and travel-inspired flavors. If that happens, he’s the kind of customer who buys again, joins the rewards club, and posts about it.

sections.html: Low involvement, but not automatic: limited problem solving. Carlos knows NA drinks but doesn't know Ar0und yet. He's skeptical, he thinks many NA drinks are overpriced, and his friends see what he orders, so it isn't automatic. One drink at the bar on a bartender's word lowers the risk, and after some good experiences, ordering it becomes routine. Our job is to make the first one low risk and easy to access.

blocks.html: Causal Upcale Restaurants
Grocery Stores with Non-Alcoholic Sections

Its not just another mocktail, it's got real flavor built around a story. It fits right in on a cocktail menue and can be priced like one, without anyone having to spend hours developing a zero-proof recipe from scratch.
Grocery stores are interested because non-alcoholic cocktails are a fast growing drink right now, and next to the plain seltzer or basic mixers Ar0und stands out.

A restaurant or grocery store is buying cases because their customers want it, they arent the ones drinking it. And its not an impulse buy on their end, they're going to taste it, compare to other options, and talk through pricing before committing to anything.

sections.title: What Makes it a Business Market:

blocks.html: Way fewer buyers than individual customers, but each one orders a lot more at once. The demand only exists because it is tied to someone else wanting it further down the line. A restaurant doesn't want Ar0und for itself, it wants it because diners are asking for it. And once it's on the menu or the shelf, that's not a one time sale, it turns into an actual relationship you have to keep up.

sections.title: What Kind of Purchase is it:

blocks.html: The first order is risky for them since they've never carried the brand before, so it would be a new buy. Once it's actually selling, reordering becomes easy and routine. If down the line they want to switch up flavors or order size, that's a modified rebuy.

sections.title: What We Bring to the Table:

blocks.html: For a restaurant, it means no recipe testing and the same quality every single time.
For a grocery store, it's a product that's already proven to sell well in a category that's taking off, so there's a lot less guesswork involved.

That is the strongest opportunity for a small, bartender-led, global recipe brand.

blocks.html: We face the question of whether Ar0und should put its first marketing dollars into the on-premise bartender partnership program (training, incentives, in-venue placement with partner bars) before spending comparable money on retail distribution and digital or social advertising.

sections.html: Most of our go-to-market plan rests on the claim that the experience of a bartender personally recommending the drink, does more to convert a hesitant customer than anything else, more than menu placement, price, or an ad would. We know the category is growing and we know our word of mouth matters to our customers, but we don’t know how much a bartender’s in-person recommendation actually moves someone from consideration to ordering, compared to just reading a good menu description or seeing a lower price.

To find out how much a bartender’s personal, in-person recommendation actually changes a target customer’s odds of ordering an unfamiliar non-alcoholic cocktail, relative to seeing the same drink listed on a menu or a store shelf with no recommendation.
Adults 21-34 who drink once a week or less are more likely to order a new non-alcoholic cocktail when a bartender recommends it than when they only see it on a menu or a store shelf.

The market exists and is growing fast. Non-alcoholic beer, wine and spirits passed $1 billion in U.S. store sales in 2025 (NIQ, via BeverageDaily). Ready-to-drink NA cocktails grew 123% in the year to August 2025 and now make up 64% of NA spirits sales (NIQ). Independent restaurants added NA drinks to their menus 47% more in January 2026 than a year earlier (SpotOn, via Business Wire).

Our target still goes out, and they listen to bartenders. Adults 21 to 34 went out for a drink 5.7 times in three months, versus 1.4 times for adults 55 and older. 38% of Gen Z ask for the bartender's recommendation every or almost every time they buy a cocktail, 10 points above the average guest, and 74% of bartenders say guests order what they recommend (CGA by NIQ). Legal-age Gen Z isn't quitting either: 74% had a drink in the past six months and 84% had a mixed drink (YPulse, citing IWSR, 2026). IWSR counts only legal-age drinkers, which is why it runs higher than Gallup's 50% for all 18 to 34 year olds on Page 1. At bars, NA cocktails are already the most-ordered NA drink: 9% of guests had one in the past three months (NIQ, 2025).

State laws differ. Under federal rules, drinks under 0.5% ABV are not alcoholic beverages and can be labeled "non-alcoholic" or "alcohol free," so many NA drinks contain trace alcohol. Ar0und is a true 0.0%. There is no national rule on who can buy NA drinks: 39 states had no statewide policy on selling them to minors (NPR, 2024). Michigan sells NA beer only to people 18 and older but requires no license for NA wine and spirits under 0.5% (Michigan Liquor Control Commission). In New York, bill S3836 would let licensed liquor stores sell NA versions of alcoholic drinks. For Ar0und, that means checking the rules in each launch state, selling 21+ only, and leaning on bars and grocery stores before liquor stores in New York.
The gap: none of this tells us whether a bartender's word moves our target to order a new NA cocktail instead of just reading the menu or seeing it on a shelf. That is the question our survey tests.

blocks.html: Before we commit real money to bartender training and royalties instead of a cheaper paid social push or a retail-first launch, we need primary data from our own target. We started with a short online survey (Page 3) because it is the fastest and cheapest of the three primary methods. If the survey supports the hypothesis, the next steps are an ethnographic study and a simple A/B test in two or three partner bars, comparing how often guests order Ar0und when a bartender recommends it versus when it only sits on the menu.

blocks.text: What has to be true for our plan to work:

blocks.html: Our hypothesis is the main test, but three other things also have to hold before the bartender plan is worth the money. The survey checks each one:
1. The hypothesis itself: a bartender recommendation beats a menu or a store shelf
2. Reach: our target goes out often enough to meet a bartender .
3. Repeat: after a first try at the bar, they would buy again somewhere we sell
4. Positioning: global recipes and a not-too-sweet taste are what they care about

The hypothesis can be true and still not justify the budget if reach or repeat fails. So these extra checks build on it: they decide how much to put behind bartenders, not whether bartenders matter. If the hypothesis fails, that budget moves to retail distribution and paid content before launch, not after.

Survey Objective was to find out whether adults 21-34 who drink once a week or less are more likely to order or buy a new non-alcoholic cocktail when a bartender recommends it than when they see it on a menu or a store shelf, and whether they go out often enough for a bartender-led business model to reach them.

blocks.html: Surveys are the fastest and cheapest way to collect primary data. Google Forms is free, it's anonymous, and every answer can be easily exported.

sections.html: Q1) Demographic. Screening. The goal was to focus on our target audience of ages 21-34. This is the data we are primarily focused on.
Q2) Geographic. Focuses on the region where our data is coming from.
Q3) Geographic. Focuses on whether our target lives where there are enough bars for a bartender-led model.
Q4) Behavioral. Looks at usage rates, from moderate drinkers to heavy drinkers to non-drinkers.
Q5) Behavioral. Looks at how often people go out, so we know if the bartender channel actually reaches them.

Q6) Hypothesis. Tests whether people are more likely to buy a new non-alcoholic cocktail when a bartender recommends it than when they see it on a menu, a store shelf, or a friend's post through social media
Q7) Psychographic. Agree/disagree statements on global flavors, how their drink looks, drinking less, and whether non-alcoholic drinks are too sweet, which shapes how we position Ar0und.
Q8) Behavioral. Where they would buy it again, so we know whether to add grocery and liquor stores after bars.

sections.html: Google Forms records every response with a chart for each question automatically. All answers also go into a linked Google Sheet, one row per person, which we filter to our target and download as Excel.

items: 30 of our 51 responses were under 21, so we screened them out. Most of the rest are Northeast college students aged 21-24, one respondent was 35-44, and no one aged 25-34 has answered yet which is a big part of our target audience.
People say they'd buy things they never actually buy.
A small sample: only 15 people fit our exact target, so the results are pretty limited.

blocks.text: Next Step: Study in Partner Bars

blocks.html: If we had more time, we would run a study, watching customers in their natural setting instead of asking them. It fits Ar0und because ours is a social drink, and how people order and share drinks with friends is something a survey can't capture. A survey tells us what people say they would do but an observation shows what they actually do. We would partner with 2-3 bars in the Finger Lakes area, put Ar0und on the menu, and spend nights watching how guests order.

items: Bartender vs. menu: How many guests order Ar0und after a bartender recommends it, compared with guests who just see it on the menu
Who orders it: Rough age, whether they're also drinking alcohol that night, and whether they're in a group or alone
When they order it: Early in the night, between alcoholic drinks, or as the last drink of the night
Group influence: Whether one person ordering it leads friends to order it too
Reactions: Whether guests post it, finish it, and order a second one
Questions guests ask: What they want to know

sections.html: Observation would be the next step to confirm what our survey suggests

How will we collect useful information that helps answer our marketing research question?

We collect useful information with a short anonymous Google Forms survey that screens for our target, compares how likely they are to buy in each situation, and records every answer in a spreadsheet we can filter

blocks.html: We see the likelihood of recommendations from bartenders vs. the likelihood of purchase from a grocery or liquor store shelf. In our findings, we had 5 responses for "very likely" to get a drink a bartender recommends, compared with 0 "very likely" responses for grocery/liquor store influence on purchase.
This supports the idea that bartender lift is important for getting new customers to try Ar0und for the first time over just supplying the store's stock.

61.9% of our responders reported that they go to a bar or cocktail restaurant at least 1-3 times a month at the minimum. On-Premise reach is going to be influential for our brand, as many seem to be going out to bars/cocktail restaurants frequently.
Our highest response for most likely to repeat purchase a non-alcoholic beverage was "At bar or restaurant" with 54.8%. Following that was 28.6% for "At the grocery store".
With our highest percentage of respondents being likely to repeat purchase on-premise, like before, we want to focus much of our marketing energy towards bartenders/restaurants/bars for our brand.

sections.html: In our target (the 15 people aged 21-34 who drink once a week or less), the average likelihood to order was 2.47 out of 5 when a bartender recommends it, versus 1.67 on a store shelf: a Bartender Lift of +0.80. 10 of the 15 rated the bartender higher than the shelf, and nobody out of all 51 respondents gave the shelf a 4 or 5. Across all 51 respondents, the lift is biggest for people who go out weekly (+1.31) and smallest for people who go out less than once a month (+0.33).

27% of our target go out less than once a month; a bartender-led launch would miss about a quarter of them, and they need another route such as grocery stores or online. Overall interest is also low: only 20% of our target gave the bartender a 4 or 5, so a recommendation helps, but it does not make the sale on its own.

sections.text: How Results could change our STP decisions:

sections.html: Segmentation: If 25-34 year old city dwellers respond more strongly than 21-24 year old college students, we must split up our segment into 2 narrower sections.
Targeting: If our sober individual segment responds more strongly than moderating customers, we must revise "The Decision We Changed".

Positioning: Only 20% of all 51 respondents agree that most non-alcoholic drinks are too sweet, while 73% enjoy food and drinks from other countries. So we lead with authentic global recipes and keep "not too sweet" as a secondary message.

Marketing mix and B2B: Our results decide where the budget goes(Bartenders or in-store sampling). Business buyers we approach first will depend on where we are aiming our marketing strategy (Restaurant vs. Grocery Store).

head: Potential Survery Finding
Marketing Interpretation
Strategic Response
rows: 1: Our target rates a bartender recommnedation higher than a store shelf, and most visit bars at least monthly.
The bartender moment from Unit 2 is real and reachable.
Launch on-premise first: sign 3-5 partner restaurants for a 90-day trial, fund the bartender royalty and pour stories, and track orders as a KPI.
2: Bartender and shelf score about the same, but "a friend posts about it" scores the highest.
Trust comes more from peers than from staff; reference groups beat opinion leaders.
Shift budget towards creators and #SipTheWorld user-generated content plus in-store sampling; keep bartenders as a supporting channel without a heavy royalty.
3: Our target likes the bartender option but goes out less than once a month, and most would rebuy at a grocery store.
The preference is real, but the bar channel cannot deliver volume.
Use bars for discovery and trial, but plan repeat purchase through the grocery NA section and our online store while approaching grocery stores.

sections.html: Our biggest limitation is a convenience sample. 30 of our 51 responses were under 21, almost everyone else is a 21-24 college student in the Northeast, and nobody aged 25-34 answered. People also report what they say they would do, not what they actually buy. Next, we would run an ethnographic study in two or three partner bars, then a small test market using the 90-day B2B trial from Unit 2.

sections.caption: Our Conclusion
rows: #1 Target Market Insight
Our customers are moderators, not quitters. They still go out; they just want something worth ordering.
Selected Target Market
Moderating Explorers: adults 21-34 who drink once a week or less and still go out with friends.
Most Important Research Question
Does a bartender's recommendation make our target more likely to order than seeing Ar0und on a menu or a store shelf?
Most Valuable Survey Measure
Bartender Lift (bartender likelihood minus shelf likelihood in our target): +0.80 so far (2.47 vs 1.67 out of 5).
Next Strategic Decision
Whether to commit our launch budget to partner bartenders or lead with retail and online.
